articles.title: What Is Live Rosin? Everything to Know About Hash Rosin Gummies
articles.dek: Fresh-frozen flower, an ice-water wash, heat and pressure: here's what live rosin is, how it stacks up against resin and distillate, and why it sits at the heart of every Hashables gummy.
articles.metaDescription: Live rosin is a solventless extract made from fresh-frozen cannabis with ice, cold water, heat and pressure. See how it compares to resin and distillate.
articles.body:
Live rosin is a solventless extract made from fresh-frozen cannabis flower using only ice, cold water, heat and pressure. No butane, no ethanol, no chemical solvents at any step. A hash rosin gummy is infused with that rosin instead of distillate, and it's the foundation of every Hashables gummy.

Below, we unpack each word in the name, line live rosin up against the other extracts on a dispensary menu, and explain why it makes such a flavorful gummy.

What does live rosin mean?

The name tells you how it's made, one word at a time.

  • Live means the plant was frozen fresh at harvest, skipping the usual drying and curing. Freezing helps preserve delicate aromatic compounds that drying can fade, so the extract stays closer to the scent of the living plant.
  • Rosin is the oil pressed out of cannabis with heat and pressure alone. Because it's a mechanical extract, it belongs to the solventless family.
  • Hash rosin is rosin pressed from hash, most often ice-water hash (a concentrate of the plant's resin glands), rather than straight from the flower.

Put it together and live hash rosin follows a simple path: fresh-frozen flower becomes ice-water hash, and that hash is pressed into rosin. For the step-by-step version, read Fresh Pressed, Explained.

Live rosin vs. live resin vs. distillate

Dispensary menus are full of extract names that sound alike. Here's how the three you'll see most often actually differ.

  • Live rosin: made from fresh-frozen flower, separated with ice and water, then pressed with heat and pressure. No solvents at any point.
  • Live resin: also made from fresh-frozen material, but extracted with a chemical solvent, usually a hydrocarbon such as butane or propane, which is purged out afterward. One letter apart from rosin, a whole different process.
  • Distillate: an extract refined through distillation until it's mostly THC. The process leaves most of the plant's natural aroma behind, so distillate tastes like very little on its own.

Hashables skip distillate entirely. The hash gives every gummy a distinct flower flavor that distillate simply can't deliver.

Why does solventless matter?

Solvent-based extraction uses a chemical solvent to dissolve the plant's resin, and that solvent then has to be removed before the extract is finished. In regulated markets, licensed labs screen those products for leftover solvents before they can be sold.

Solventless extraction keeps chemicals out of the picture from the start. Cold makes the resin glands brittle enough to snap off in ice water, then heat and pressure squeeze out the oil. What's left is the plant's own resin, concentrated, and that simplicity is a big part of rosin's appeal.

What makes a hash rosin gummy different?

Plenty of cannabis gummies are made with distillate because it's consistent and nearly flavorless. A hash rosin gummy starts from a full-spectrum extract instead, and you can taste it.

  • Flavor: rosin carries the plant's terpenes, the aromatic compounds behind cannabis's scent. In Hashables, that comes through as a distinct flower flavor layered with natural flavors.
  • Full spectrum: rosin keeps a broad mix of cannabinoids and terpenes together instead of isolating THC. Hashables are full-spectrum edibles with a broad cannabinoid profile.
  • Process: the extract goes from flower to rosin without a solvent or a distillation step.

Across the core lineup, every flavor delivers the same easygoing, uplifting chill, so you can choose purely by taste. Effects vary from person to person; if you're new, read Start Low, Go Slow first.

Hashables: New England's own fresh-pressed gummy

Hashables is a Nova Farms brand, and it's built by hash makers: the hash is the base of every gummy. It starts with fresh-frozen flower from Nova's own farms, which becomes ice-water hash and then fresh-pressed live rosin.

Nova has been making Hashables for years, and they're one of the first live rosin gummies in the Northeast. Along the way, Tropical Typhoon was named Sugar Confections Winner at the 2023 Harvest Cup, and Watermelon Jolt took Second Place for Sativa Gummies at the High Times Cannabis Cup Massachusetts: People's Choice Edition 2022.

Browse all Hashables live rosin gummies, or take the tasting tour in our flavor field guide.

articles.title: Fresh Pressed, Explained: From Frozen Flower to Live Rosin Gummy
articles.dek: Ice, cold water, heat and pressure: here's how Hashables go from farm flower to fresh-pressed gummy, one solventless step at a time.
articles.metaDescription: How is live rosin made? Follow fresh-frozen flower through the ice-water wash and the rosin press into a solventless Hashables gummy, step by step.
articles.body:
Fresh pressed means the rosin in every Hashables gummy is pressed from ice-water hash, and that hash is made from fresh-frozen flower. The whole extraction runs on four things: ice, cold water, heat and pressure. Here's how a harvest becomes a stack of gummies.

Every solventless hash maker has its own craft and fine-tuning, but the basic steps look like this.

Step 1: Fresh-frozen farm flower

Hashables begin with flower from Nova Farms' own farms. An extract can only be as good as the plant behind it, so the whole process starts on the farm.

At harvest, the path splits in two:

  • Dried and cured: the usual route for flower that's meant to be smoked. It takes time, and some of the plant's most delicate aromas fade along the way.
  • Fresh frozen: the route to live rosin. The flower is frozen fresh instead of dried, which helps hold on to its aroma. That's what puts the live in live rosin.

Freezing also keeps the trichomes intact. These tiny, mushroom-shaped resin glands frost every bud, and they're where the plant concentrates its cannabinoids and terpenes.

Step 2: The ice-water wash

Next comes the wash. The frozen flower is gently stirred in ice and cold water, and the cold makes the trichome heads brittle enough to snap off and sink, while the leaves and stems stay behind.

The water is then filtered through a series of fine mesh screens that catch the trichome heads by size. What's collected is ice-water hash, a sandy, golden concentrate of resin glands, and it's dried before it heads to the press.

Step 3: Pressing hash into rosin

The dried hash is tucked into a fine mesh filter bag and pressed between heated plates. Gentle heat and steady pressure push the oil out through the mesh and leave the spent material behind.

That oil is live hash rosin. No chemical touches it at any point, which is exactly what solventless means.

Fresh rosin can range from a glossy, golden oil to a soft, buttery paste, depending on the plant and how it's handled after pressing. Either way, every drop came from the flower.

Step 4: From rosin to gummy

Finally, the rosin is carefully dosed into the gummy along with natural flavors, and the gummies are set into cubes. Instead of distillate, every Hashables gummy carries solventless hash rosin, so each bite brings a distinct flower flavor alongside the fruit flavor.

Then it's stacks on stacks of flavor, from Tropical Typhoon to Prickly Pear. Take the tasting tour in our flavor field guide.

Why fresh pressed matters

Plenty of edibles take a different route: a solvent pulls a crude extract from the plant, and that extract is then distilled until it's mostly THC. Fresh pressed skips both steps, and that changes the gummy in three ways:

  • Flavor: freezing at harvest helps keep the plant's aroma, and the hash brings a flower flavor you can't get from distillate.
  • Full spectrum: rosin keeps a broad mix of cannabinoids and terpenes together, which is why Hashables are full-spectrum edibles with a broad cannabinoid profile.
  • Simplicity: ice, cold water, heat and pressure make up the entire toolkit for the extract. Easy to understand, start to finish.

It's a process Nova has been running for years, and Hashables are one of the first live rosin gummies in the Northeast. Read more in our story, or see how rosin compares to other extracts in What Is Live Rosin?

articles.title: Why Are Cannabis Edibles Lab Tested? What the Lab Checks For
articles.dek: Before a legal gummy reaches the dispensary shelf, an independent lab checks what's in it and what shouldn't be: here's how that works and what it means for you.
articles.metaDescription: Why are edibles lab tested? See what licensed labs check, from THC potency to pesticides and mold, and how to read a certificate of analysis (COA).
articles.body:
Cannabis edibles are lab tested to confirm two things: that the potency on the label is accurate, and that contaminants such as pesticides, heavy metals and mold are within safety limits. In regulated markets like Massachusetts, state rules require a licensed, independent lab to test cannabis products before they can be sold. For edibles, where you're trusting the label to tell you how much THC is in each piece, that check matters.

Who tests cannabis edibles?

Testing is done by licensed labs that operate independently of the companies whose products they test. In Massachusetts, the Cannabis Control Commission licenses these labs and sets the standards they test against. On top of a state license, testing labs are typically accredited to an international quality standard for laboratories.

That independence is the point. Because the lab isn't the company that made the product, its results act as an outside check, and a batch that fails can't be sold as is.

What does a cannabis lab test check for?

Exact requirements vary by state, but testing for edibles generally covers:

  • Potency: how much THC, CBD and other cannabinoids the product contains.
  • Pesticides: screening for residues from crop treatments.
  • Heavy metals: such as lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury, which plants can absorb from soil and water.
  • Microbes: including mold, yeast and harmful bacteria.
  • Mycotoxins: toxins that certain molds can produce.
  • Residual solvents: leftovers from solvent-based extraction, for products made that way.

Each result is measured against limits set by the state. A batch has to clear them before it can move on toward a dispensary shelf.

Why does potency testing matter for edibles?

With edibles, the label is your dosing guide. Effects can take up to two hours or more to arrive, so it's easy to take more too soon, and an inaccurate number would only make that guesswork harder.

Potency testing measures the cannabinoids in a batch, which is how the number on the package gets checked against what's actually inside. Because testing happens batch by batch, the results describe the batch in your hand, not one made months earlier.

One thing a lab report can't tell you is how an edible will feel for you. That depends on your body, your tolerance and your timing, which is why starting low and going slow still matters.

Does solventless rosin still get tested?

Yes. Solvent-based extracts are screened for leftover solvents because a chemical was used to make them. Solventless hash rosin, the extract in every Hashables gummy, is made with ice, cold water, heat and pressure, so no extraction solvent enters the process at all.

But solventless doesn't mean skipping the lab. Under state rules, every licensed edible, Hashables included, goes through required testing before it can be sold. Solventless describes how the extract is made; testing is how everyone gets to verify the finished product.

How to read a cannabis lab report

A lab's report is called a certificate of analysis, or COA. If you're looking at one, here's what to check:

  • The lab: it should be a licensed, independent testing lab.
  • The batch or lot number: it should match the one on your package.
  • The test date: results apply to the specific batch that was tested.
  • Potency: THC and other cannabinoids, often shown as a percentage or in milligrams.
  • Safety results: pass or fail for pesticides, heavy metals, microbes and mycotoxins.

Your package label lists the product's THC content too. Still have questions? Ask your budtender, visit our lab results page or contact us.

articles.title: What Is the Entourage Effect? Terpenes and Full Spectrum, Explained
articles.dek: Cannabis is a whole crew of compounds, not a solo act: here's what terpenes, full-spectrum extracts and the much-debated entourage effect are all about.
articles.metaDescription: What is the entourage effect? Learn what terpenes and full-spectrum extracts are, where the idea came from, and what science can and can't say yet.
articles.body:
The entourage effect is the idea that cannabis compounds work better as a team than alone: that THC, the plant's other cannabinoids and its aromatic terpenes shape the experience together. It's widely discussed, but researchers are still working out how much of it holds up, so think of it as a theory rather than settled science. Full-spectrum extracts like hash rosin are made to keep that whole team together.

What are terpenes?

Terpenes are aromatic compounds made by many plants. They're behind the smell of citrus peel, pine needles, lavender and black pepper, and cannabis produces dozens of its own, mostly in the frosty resin glands called trichomes.

A few that commonly turn up in cannabis:

  • Myrcene: earthy and musky, also found in mango and lemongrass.
  • Limonene: bright and citrusy, a major part of lemon and orange peel.
  • Pinene: fresh and piney, just as the name suggests.
  • Linalool: soft and floral, best known from lavender.
  • Beta-caryophyllene: peppery and warm, also found in black pepper and cloves.

Each cultivar carries its own mix, which is a big reason one batch of cannabis can smell like a lemon grove and the next like a pine forest.

Terpenes are also volatile, which means they evaporate easily with heat and time. That's one reason live rosin starts with flower that's frozen fresh instead of dried.

What does full-spectrum mean?

A full-spectrum extract carries a broad range of what the plant makes: THC along with other cannabinoids, terpenes and other natural compounds. The aim is to bring the plant's chemistry along as a set, rather than pulling out a single compound.

Besides THC and CBD, cannabis makes smaller amounts of so-called minor cannabinoids, such as CBG and CBC. Another one, CBN, mostly forms as THC ages.

You'll also run into two other extract types:

  • Distillate is refined until it's mostly THC, and much of the plant's natural terpene content is lost along the way. Some products add flavor or terpenes back in afterward.
  • Isolate is a single cannabinoid, such as CBD, purified on its own.

Hashables are full-spectrum edibles with a broad cannabinoid profile. Instead of distillate, every gummy is dosed with solventless hash rosin, which keeps the plant's cannabinoids and terpenes together.

Where does the entourage effect idea come from?

The term dates to 1998. That year, a paper co-authored by Raphael Mechoulam, the Israeli chemist known for his pioneering work on THC, used it to describe compounds in the body that do little on their own but boost the activity of one of the body's own cannabinoids.

Since then, the phrase has been borrowed for the whole cannabis plant: the notion that terpenes and minor cannabinoids might shape how THC feels. It's a popular explanation for why two products with the same THC number can feel different, but scientists are still studying whether, and how, it works.

What it means for a Hashables gummy

The easiest place to notice full spectrum is flavor. The hash gives Hashables a distinct flower flavor that distillate can't match, layered with natural flavors in every cube.

Hashables are made to keep the plant's cannabinoids and terpenes together, the combination the entourage effect is all about. What we can say for sure is how they're made: fresh-frozen farm flower, washed into hash and pressed into solventless rosin, with no distillate in sight. Across the core lineup, every flavor delivers the same uplifting chill.

Everyone responds differently, so if you're new to edibles, read Start Low, Go Slow before your first bite. For the extraction side of the story, see What Is Live Rosin?

articles.title: Stacks on Stacks: A Field Guide to Every Hashables Flavor
articles.dek: Nine flavors, one fresh-pressed base: here's a tasting tour of the whole Hashables lineup, from award winners to limited runs.
articles.metaDescription: A tasting guide to every Hashables live rosin gummy: five core flavors, two specialty picks and two limited editions, plus what prickly pear tastes like.
articles.body:
Hashables come in nine flavors: five year-round core flavors, two specialty gummies (one for sleep, one sugar-free) and two limited editions that are here while they last. Every one is made with fresh-pressed, solventless hash rosin. Across the core lineup the experience is the same uplifting chill, so picking a favorite comes down to taste.

Think of the tasting notes below as postcards, not recipes: they describe how each flavor tastes, not what goes into it. Tastes like paradise, nine different ways.

The core five: year-round Hashables flavors

These are the flavors that define Hashables, and they're here all year. See the core lineup.

Tropical Typhoon

Think a tropical storm of fruit blowing in off the water: ripe pineapple and mango up front, with a tangy swirl on the finish. It was named Sugar Confections Winner at the 2023 Harvest Cup in Worcester, Massachusetts, and took Third Place in Edibles: Sativa Gummies at the High Times Cannabis Cup Massachusetts: People's Choice Edition 2023. Meet Tropical Typhoon.

Bangin' Berry

Think a sun-warmed handful of mixed berries: raspberry brightness, blackberry depth and a sweet strawberry finish, all landing at once. Big, bold and berry all the way through. Meet Bangin' Berry.

Watermelon Jolt

Think the first bite of an ice-cold watermelon wedge on a scorching afternoon, with a bright little jolt of tang to wake it up. It took Second Place for Sativa Gummies at the High Times Cannabis Cup Massachusetts: People's Choice Edition 2022. Meet Watermelon Jolt.

Peachy Mango

Think a ripe peach and a golden mango sharing one cube: soft, juicy and sunny, like the last warm hour before sunset. Meet Peachy Mango.

Electric Grape

Think deep purple grape with a zippy, candy-bright edge, the flavor version of heat lightning on a summer night. Meet Electric Grape.

Specialty flavors: sleep and sugar-free

The two specialty gummies are here to stay alongside the core five, each with its own twist. See the specialty flavors.

Remberry (sleep)

Remberry is the Hashables sleep gummy, made for the end of the day. Think dark berries under a full moon: deep, jammy and mellow.

The sleep formula pairs THC hash rosin with CBD and CBN isolates. In some markets it's finished with a touch of melatonin and in others it's melatonin-free, so check the pack. Meet Remberry.

Blue Raspberry (sugar-free)

Blue Raspberry is the sugar-free pick. Think the sweet, tangy blue raspberry of a boardwalk snow cone, minus the sugar. Meet Blue Raspberry.

Limited editions: here while they last

These two are limited runs, so when they're gone, they may not be back. If one catches your eye, don't wait too long. See the limited editions.

Lemon Burst

Think a fresh-cut lemon on a blazing afternoon: sunny, zesty and just tart enough to make you pucker. Meet Lemon Burst.

Prickly Pear

Think juicy watermelon meets ripe berry, with a soft, floral sweetness that's hard to place and easy to love. Meet Prickly Pear.

What does prickly pear taste like?

Prickly pear is the fruit of the Opuntia cactus, the paddle-shaped cactus that grows across Mexico and the American Southwest. Under a skin covered in tiny spines, the fruit hides juicy flesh that can be green, golden or vivid magenta, dotted with small, hard seeds.

The flavor is mild, sweet and refreshing, and it's often compared to a mix of watermelon and berry. That's the profile Hashables Prickly Pear plays on: think a desert fruit with a beach-day attitude.

articles.title: Start Low, Go Slow: A First-Timer's Guide to Edibles
articles.dek: Edibles reward patience: here's how to read the label, why the effects take their sweet time, and the simple rules that keep a first time easy.
articles.metaDescription: New to edibles? Start low and go slow: effects can take two hours or more to arrive. Here's how to read the label, wait it out and store gummies safely.
articles.body:
The golden rule for a first time with edibles is simple: start low and go slow. Take a small amount, then wait, because the effects of an edible can take up to two hours or more to arrive. Taking more before the first serving kicks in is the classic way to overdo it.

Why do edibles take so long to kick in?

When cannabis is smoked or vaped, THC enters the bloodstream through the lungs within minutes. An edible takes the scenic route: it's digested, absorbed through the gut and processed by the liver before it reaches the bloodstream and brain.

Along the way, the liver converts some THC into a related compound called 11-hydroxy-THC, which is one reason edibles can feel different from smoking. The slow trip through the body also means the effects tend to last longer, often for several hours.

Timing varies from person to person, too. What you've eaten, your metabolism and your tolerance can all change how fast an edible arrives and how strong it feels.

How to start low: read the label first

Every legal edible sold in a regulated market carries a state-required label with its THC content. Before you take anything, find the potency per serving and per package, and check how much THC is in a single piece.

  • Start small. If you're new, take less than you think you need. You can always take more another day, but you can't take less once it's in.
  • Ask your budtender. They can walk you through the label and help you choose a low starting point.
  • Take notes. Jot down how much you took, when, and how it felt, so your next time is easier to plan.

How to go slow: give it time

  • Wait at least two hours before you even think about taking more. If you're new, save seconds for another day.
  • Pick a comfortable setting: somewhere familiar and relaxed, with nowhere you need to be.
  • Clear your schedule. Effects can last for hours, so plan a hammock-and-sunset kind of afternoon, not a to-do list.
  • Have water and a snack within reach, and let the rest of the day stay easy.

If you do overdo it, remember that the feeling is temporary. Find a calm, comfortable spot, sip some water and rest. If you feel seriously unwell, call 911 or get medical help.

Edible safety basics

  • Adults 21 and over only. Adult-use cannabis is for people 21 and older.
  • Never drive. Don't drive or operate machinery after an edible, and skip swimming, surfing or anything else that needs your full attention.
  • Keep them away from kids and pets. Gummies can look like regular candy, so store them in their original package, up high or locked away.
  • Store them cool and dry, away from heat and direct sun, so they keep their shape and flavor.
  • No mixing. Don't combine edibles with other substances.
  • Check with your doctor first if you take medication, and skip cannabis entirely if you're pregnant or breastfeeding.

If a child or pet eats an edible, call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 or your vet right away. In an emergency, call 911.

Choosing your first Hashables

Across the core lineup, every Hashables flavor delivers the same uplifting chill, so for a first time you can pick purely by taste. Check the potency on the state label, ask your budtender for a starting point and give it time. Browse the lineup in our flavor field guide, or find answers to common questions in our FAQs.
